newsitem.title: INDIA: India uproar postpones Chidambaram's budget speech.
newsitem.headline: India uproar postpones Chidambaram's budget speech.

text.p: Political upheaval in a western Indian state forced Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Tuesday to postpone an eagerly awaited speech on the federal budget, disappointing stock markets.
Chidambaram had planned to address parliament on the proposed 1996/97 (April-March) budget.
Markets, banking on sweeteners for selected sectors, were expecting him to offer concessions to industries which have lobbied his office since he presented the blueprint in July.
But members of the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), in an uproar over a split in the Hindu nationalist party in Gujarat state, forced repeated adjournment of both houses of parliament.

BJP lawmakers were protesting against a decision by the deputy speaker of the Gujarat assembly to recognise a breakaway faction of the right-wing party, which has been shaken by rivalries in the western state.
BJP parliamentarians accused Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition of helping to engineer the Gujarat split.
Speaking into an uninterrupted din of catcalls, Chidambaram made a brief announcement on cotton fabric excise duties and then withdrew.
A senior aide said he was prepared to address the budget on Wednesday provided the protest died down.
The postponement of Chidambaram's budget remarks frustrated Indian stock markets, which tumbled on news of a U.S. missile attack on Iraq.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark index fell 78.30 points, or 2.20 percent, to close at 3,484.68.
"To a certain extent I'm disappointed," a Bombay-based broker said. "But this will keep expectations afloat."

Aides said Chidambaram might announce concessions next week when he plans to make a second, more detailed statement on the budget, which the government wants to push through parliament by September 13 when the current session is set to end.

Markets anticipate Chidambaram will exempt some selected industries from a minimum corporate tax which the government says will help generate more tax revenue from companies, many of which currently pay no taxes.
